title: St Patrick (17 March)
hook: the breastplate prayer: Christ with me, Christ before me, Christ behind me

segments.voice: Yesterday, three forties: Moses, Elijah, Jesus, and each one with a far side. Your line was forty is enough. What did you choose to keep? Day one thousand twenty-three.

Green rivers, marching bands, plastic hats, a parade down the main street of cities that are nowhere near Ireland. That's one St Patrick's day. There's another, much quieter, and it starts with a short piece of writing by the man himself. In it he doesn't sound like a hero. He sounds embarrassed. He says he was not a learned man, that he writes clumsily, that as a young man he didn't really know God. And then he tells how he was stolen from his home, carried across the sea and made a slave in a strange country. The parade remembers a national saint. His own words remember a kidnapped boy. Today, St Patrick.
screen: `A SHORT ACCOUNT BY THE MAN HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: Patrick's own account is called his Confession, and it's worth hearing in outline. He grew up in Britain, in a Christian family, but he says he paid its faith little attention. Raiders took him captive to Ireland, where he was set to watch flocks on the hillsides. And there, alone, cold and hungry, he began to pray, he says, day and night, in snow and frost and rain. After years of this, a voice in his sleep told him a ship was ready. He ran, found the ship, and got home. That should be the end. Instead he dreams of a man bringing letters, and one of them is headed the voice of the Irish, calling him, as he tells it, to come and walk among them again. And he goes back. Back to the country of his slavery, to spend his life there. That's the man the prayer is pinned to. Tradition gives Patrick a hymn called the Breastplate, a prayer you put on like armor before going out. Whether he wrote it himself is uncertain; it isn't in his Confession. But it sounds like someone who knows what it is to be alone in a hostile place. Its familiar lines, in one English version, go: Christ with me, Christ before me, Christ behind me, Christ in me, Christ beneath me, Christ above me, Christ on my right, Christ on my left. Every direction is covered. Nowhere is left empty. Some readers hear in it the shepherd boy on the hillside, finding out he was never actually alone. The shamrock and the snakes come later, from legend. The Confession is where the man himself speaks.
screen: `THE VOICE OF THE IRISH CALLS HIM BACK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk slowly through the directions of the breastplate. Sit or stand, and breathe. Notice what's in front of you. Then behind. Then the ground beneath you, the sky or ceiling above, your right side, your left. Take your time with each one. If you pray, you can say the lines as you go: Christ before me, Christ behind me, Christ beneath me, Christ above me, Christ beside me. If you don't, simply notice that you are held on every side, by the floor, the air, the room, the people somewhere near. Then rest in the middle of it. The bell holds the time.
St Patrick. A boy taken as a slave to Ireland who escaped, then chose to go back, and whose name is tied to a prayer that fills every direction with Christ.
Your line: christ beside me. Today, when you walk into a room that makes you nervous, notice who and what is beside you before you speak. Day one thousand twenty-three.

howItsDone: Catholic and Anglican churches, and some others, keep St Patrick's feast with services and prayers, and the Breastplate is sung as a hymn or said as a morning prayer in some churches; in Ireland it is also a national holiday.

fork.setup: you're Patrick. you escaped slavery and you're home, safe. then you dream of the Irish, calling you to come back and walk among them. what do you do?
options: stay home; you've earned your safety.
go back to the country of your slavery.
fork.reveal: he went back. by his own account, he spent his life in Ireland, the land where he had once been a slave.

trapdoor: what you thought: parades, green beer, and shamrocks.
what it means: a kidnapped boy who found God as a slave, escaped, and went back to the land of his captivity.
what a scholar hears: Patrick's Confession is his own account; the Breastplate is given to him by tradition, and its authorship is uncertain.
recall: an old word for a birth

notes: Claims rule: Patrick's age at capture, the number of years in slavery, and dates are left out; 'after years of this' paraphrases the Confession's account (it gives six years). Confirm.
Breastplate lines are given as paraphrase 'in one common English version' (close to Kuno Meyer's and others) and not cited as a quotation; confirm wording is acceptable.
'Scholars aren't sure he wrote it' — the Lorica is generally dated later than Patrick; confirm phrasing.
The Confession's dream of Victoricus and the 'voice of the Irish' paraphrased; confirm.
Original is null: the sources are Latin/Old Irish and no single word fits.

Editor 2: the Confession is not a letter, so 'the letter remembers' and 'the letter and the prayer are where the man is' reworded.

Audit: the Confessio's voices come from near the Wood of Voclut, and whether that was the place of his captivity is debated, so 'the very people who had held him' cut from teach, fork and trapdoor; hook screen 'letter' changed to 'account' to match Editor 2's note.
